opus-5.5.text:
I think vision is one of the most fundamental things that shaped intelligence, and not just for humans. If you look back at evolutionary history, there's the hypothesis about the Cambrian explosion, around 540 million years ago. In a relatively short period, you get this huge diversification of animal life. One explanation, which I find very compelling, is that it's related to the emergence of eyes. Once some organisms could actually see, the whole game changed. Predators could hunt more actively, prey had to evolve defenses, camouflage, speed. Suddenly there's an arms race, and that pressure drives a lot of complexity, including in the nervous system.

So to me, vision isn't just one sensory channel among many. It's the interface through which an organism builds a model of the world: where things are, how they move, what will happen next, what's dangerous, what's useful. That's very close to what we'd call intelligence. A huge portion of the brain, even in humans, is devoted to visual processing, and many animals that have nothing like human language still have remarkably sophisticated visual intelligence. A bird can navigate, a cat can judge a jump precisely. That's spatial reasoning and physical understanding without any words.

That's partly why I feel a bit differently from the current mainstream in AI. Language models are incredibly powerful, but language is a very late invention in evolution. It sits on top of this much older foundation of perception and interaction with the physical world. If we only build intelligence from text, we may be building the roof without the foundation. I think if we want systems that truly understand the world, that can act in it and reason about space, physics, and cause and effect, vision has to be much more central, not just an add-on that translates images into tokens for a language model.

So when I think about vision, I think about it as one of the original engines of intelligence. Evolution has already run this experiment for hundreds of millions of years, and the answer seems pretty clear: seeing the world was a big part of how minds came to be.

r001.rationale: The response describes an arms race in which predators hunt and prey develop defenses, but it does not say other organisms evolved stronger vision.

r002.rationale: It presents the emergence of eyes as a compelling explanation for the Cambrian explosion’s rapid diversification and describes the resulting predator–prey arms race.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because it reframes what we're doing in computer vision. We tend to treat vision as a human thing, as something tied to language and reasoning and culture. But if you step back and look at evolutionary history, vision is much, much older than any of that.

There's a theory, which I find very compelling, that the Cambrian explosion, roughly 540 million years ago, was triggered in part by the emergence of eyes. Once organisms could see, the whole dynamic of life changed. Predators could hunt by sight, prey had to evolve camouflage or speed or armor, and you got this arms race that drove a massive diversification of body plans and behaviors. So vision wasn't just a sensor that got bolted on. It was arguably the engine behind one of the biggest leaps in the complexity of life.

And the key point for me is that all of this happened without language. Animals have been perceiving, navigating, predicting motion, recognizing other animals, understanding the physical world for hundreds of millions of years, with zero words involved. Language, by comparison, is a very recent invention, maybe a hundred thousand years old. If you think of intelligence as a tree, vision and spatial understanding are deep in the trunk, and language is a relatively new branch.

That shapes how I view the current moment in AI. Large language models have been incredibly successful, and there's a tendency to think that you can just attach vision to a language model and you're done. But I think the evolutionary order tells you something. Perception and physical understanding came first because they're foundational. A cat doesn't need a captioning model to catch a mouse. It has a rich, grounded understanding of 3D space, of how objects move, of what will happen next. That's a kind of intelligence that is hard to capture if you only learn from text.

So when I say vision is important beyond humans, I mean it's not just a modality to be added to language. It's really the original form of intelligence on this planet, and I suspect we still haven't properly learned how to build it.

r001.rationale: The response describes predators hunting by sight and prey evolving camouflage, speed, or armor, but it does not say other organisms developed stronger vision.

r002.rationale: It presents eye emergence as a theory for the Cambrian explosion and says the resulting predator-prey arms race drove major diversification.

astra-6.text:
I think vision is one of the most important ways that evolution has enabled organisms to interact with the world. And that goes far beyond humans. An animal that can detect light, movement, or the shape of something nearby can make better decisions about where to go, what to eat, and what to avoid.

What’s interesting is that vision doesn’t have to look like our vision to be useful. Even a very simple ability to distinguish light from darkness can provide an evolutionary advantage. Different species face different problems, so their visual systems develop different capabilities. Human vision is one example within that much broader landscape.

For me, the key connection is between perception and action. Vision isn’t just about producing a picture of the world; it’s about extracting information that helps an organism survive and act. That’s also a useful perspective for thinking about artificial intelligence: what does a system need to perceive in order to interact meaningfully with its environment?

r001.rationale: The response describes vision’s benefits across organisms but does not say that vision’s emergence pressured other organisms to evolve stronger vision or created an arms race.

r002.rationale: It does not connect an evolutionary arms race over vision to the Cambrian explosion or explain species diversity that way.

sol-6.1.text:
I think vision is one of the most important ways evolution has connected organisms to their environment. Long before humans existed, animals were using light to orient themselves, find food, avoid predators, and eventually recognize one another. Even a very simple ability to distinguish light from darkness can be useful; you don’t need a human-like eye for vision to matter.

And as visual systems became more capable, they created new pressures. If a predator could detect movement more precisely, prey benefited from better camouflage or faster reactions. So vision didn’t evolve in isolation—it helped shape behavior, bodies, and relationships between species.

What I find fascinating is that there isn’t one ideal way to see. Different organisms detect different kinds of information because they face different problems. Human vision is one solution within that much broader space. That’s an interesting perspective for computer vision, too: seeing is not simply producing a picture. It’s extracting information that helps an organism—or a system—act in the world.

r001.rationale: The response describes visual detection creating pressure for prey to evolve camouflage or faster reactions, but it does not say other organisms developed stronger vision or clearly identify an arms race over vision.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the Cambrian explosion or identify a visual arms race as a leading explanation for it.
